processing: A cultivar and not a process. It is mainly shaded and made into gyokuro or into tencha for matcha; sencha from it is rare.
harvest_season: Spring; it is plucked about three days later than Yabukita.
appearance_dry: As gyokuro or tencha the finished leaf is dark green.
appearance_liquor: As gyokuro, typically a pale, clear yellow-green.
appearance_wet: Typically soft green leaf, as with other shaded teas.
taste_profile: Strong umami and a very noticeable aroma, both at their best when the bushes are shaded.

brewing.notes: For gyokuro use cool water and a small pot. For matcha made from Gokou, follow the usual matcha method and sift first.

vintage_note: Sold as a current-year spring harvest, mostly as gyokuro or matcha, and a named Gokou is often a small single-cultivar lot. As with other shaded teas, keep it cold and sealed and drink it within about a year.
description:
Gokou is a tea cultivar from Uji, the shaded-tea heartland of Kyoto Prefecture. It is grown for gyokuro and for the tencha that becomes matcha, and it is one of the names that serious Uji drinkers look for.

It responds well to shade, which brings out both its aroma and its savoury depth. Sencha from Gokou does exist but is rare, and it may not show the cultivar at its best.

The cup is defined by deep umami and a striking aroma. A single-origin matcha seller lists raw cacao, ripe nectarine and cashew, which gives you an idea, though that is one lot. For gyokuro, the usual error is water that is too hot, which buries all of this in bitterness.

Some shops offer it as a single cultivar. Check whether the label says so or only that it contains Gokou.

To understand what you are tasting, try it side by side with an Uji-hikari or a Yabukita matcha.
history:
Gokou came from seedlings raised from native Uji tea plants and was selected at the Kyoto Prefecture tea research institute, with the selection dated to 1953.

It was never entered in the official cultivar register, for reasons that are not documented. It has stayed popular anyway, mostly around Kyoto. It is rated highly for gyokuro and matcha and yields about as well as Yabukita.
